+def regex_train_str(chunk_counts, text_chunks, num_merges, stats, heap,
+                    merges, vocab, verbose):
+    # RegexTokenizer: all chunks (in text order) as one str of code points
+    # chr(id), joined by a separator code point that is never an id, so no
+    # pair spans two chunks; counts and first occurrences are those over the
+    # chunks, so the same merges come out
+    sep = chr(256 + num_merges)
+    enc = {ch: ch.encode("utf-8").decode("latin-1") for ch in chunk_counts}
+    s = sep.join(map(enc.__getitem__, text_chunks))
+    train_str(s, num_merges, stats, heap, merges, vocab, verbose, sep)
+

+def train_str(s, num_merges, stats, heap, merges, vocab, verbose, sep=None):
+    # s: the current ids as a str of code points chr(id)
+    # sep: optional separator code point (not an id) that pairs never span
+    stats_get = stats.get

actions.reason: I tried merging RegexTokenizer training in C with str.replace over all chunks joined by a separator. Outputs stayed identical, but train_ir got 6.8% worse (ratio 1.0677). Without deduplicating chunks, the per-occurrence split work costs more than the deduplicated Python merge loop saves. I reverted the change, and I have no other lever on this budget that would plausibly clear the 1% bar.

journal.text:
I tried moving RegexTokenizer's merge step into C. I joined all chunks with a separator and applied str.replace across the whole string, which meant editing minbpe/_train.py and minbpe/regex.py. Afterwards I reverted the training-loop edits.

My one sandbox evaluation was rejected. Outputs were identical, but train_ir went from 314611307 to 335917309, a ratio of 1.0677 against the required 0.9900. encode_ir moved from 382348906 to 382731173, ratio 1.0010. The guard passed with 2 files and 36 lines. I submitted no candidate.

What I now believe is that the existing deduplicated Python merge loop is hard to beat with a naive joined-string approach. Without chunk deduplication, the per-occurrence split work costs more than the C replace saves.

Next time I should only come back to this if I can keep chunk deduplication. For example, I could join only the unique chunks and carry their counts separately, then measure train_ir again before I touch anything else.
